# Mahākapijātaka (Ja 516)

**ID:** Ja 516
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Mahākapijātaka
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul15.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Mahākapijātaka* (Ja 516), also titled *The Monkey Betrayed*, is a canonical birth story recounting the Bodhisatta's past life as an ascetic monkey dwelling on Mount Himavat [Wood 2005]. According to the narrative frame, the Buddha recounted the story while residing at the Bamboo Grove after Devadatta hurled a rock at him, explaining that Devadatta had attempted to kill him with a stone in a previous life as well. In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta rescues a man stranded in the forest by carrying him up out of a chasm on his back [Wood 2005; Anandajoti 2010]. While the exhausted monkey rests, the ungrateful man attempts to murder him with a stone for food; surviving the attack, the Bodhisatta guides him out, but the traitor is subsequently afflicted with leprosy and pustulant boils before suffering destruction [Wood 2005; Anandajoti 2010; Radich 2011]. Its verses condemn treachery (*mittadubbho*), emphasizing that one should never harm a benefactor, just as one should not break the branches of a tree that affords shade [Anandajoti 2010].

In modern scholarship and Buddhist art history, this narrative is commonly designated "Mahakapi Jataka II" or the "Jātaka of the Ascetic Monkey" to distinguish it from the better-known story of the monkey king who bridges a river (Ja 407) [Spink 2007; Wood 2005]. Scenes representing the rescue and betrayal are found on a coping relief at Bhārhut and in the wall paintings of Cave 17 at Ajanta [Spink 2007; Wood 2005]. A closely related Sanskrit version appears as story twenty-seven of Āryaśūra's *Jātakamālā* [Martin 2006].

 Automatically computed matches by DharmaNexus indicate substantial Pali-internal text reuse with the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* and the *Visuddhimagga*, as well as cross-language alignments with the Tibetan translation of Āryaśūra's *Jātakamālā* (61 matches) and Sanskrit and Tibetan Mahāyāna treatises including the *Śikṣāsamuccaya* and *Dharmasamuccaya* [DharmaNexus].
